top.line: Readers should pay for a persona that follows them
top.para: Paying out of obligation, guilt or virtue works only to a degree and does not scale. Readers should pay because it helps them: time, context, focus and better decisions. Reading on this site builds personas with names and graphs, but they live in one browser, so the thing worth paying for is a persona that follows you, privately.

s0.line: Pay for a persona that follows you, not guilt
s0.para: Paywalls, guilt and donations work to a degree but do not scale. Readers should pay for time, context, focus and better decisions, which a persona delivers. Reading builds one with a name and graph, readers can keep several, and five are ready to start from. Today two devices mean two strangers, which is the problem worth paying to fix.

s1.line: Paywalls, guilt and donations work but do not scale
s1.para: Readers pay because they must, as with the Guardian app's 20 free articles a month; because they feel they must, as with its £12 tier to avoid supporter pop-ups; or because it is right, as with Wikipedia's 8 million donors averaging $10.58. All work to a degree, but not for anyone not already enormous.

s2.line: Readers buy time, context and focus, not articles
s2.para: Articles here are free even with the meter below zero. What readers buy is time, context, focus, better decisions, a streamlined way through and a better experience. All depend on one asset: a record of what was read, how far, and what was kept or rejected, which the reading meter already keeps and now acts on visibly.

s3.line: Your reading builds a named persona you can steer
s3.para: Every page read adds to a persona, weighted by how far down you read, and it is named from your topics, such as The Policy Architect. It has a newsroom of picks and a graph of topics and pages. Keep and Not for this persona buttons let the reader see and change the model the site holds.

s4.line: Several personas let readers manage focus across interests
s4.para: Building The Cyber Boardroom showed users want several personas, not one. Each has its own picks, graph and kept or rejected articles, while a default persona counts everything. Five ready-made personas start from seven or eight articles each: Morgan the founder, Rowan the journalist, Sam the security lead, Kai the AI builder and Jordan the board member.

s5.line: A second device makes you a stranger again
s5.para: On an iPad the site worked, but a laptop would show a new balance, no history and no persona. Resetting the meter in a private window is not a worry, since that reader would not pay anyway. Losing a persona gets worse as the product improves; today the only fix is a manual JSON export and restore.

s6.line: People will pay to keep their persona everywhere
s6.para: The value proposition is a persona that follows you to phone, laptop and agent, so Claude reads as your security persona when you work on security. People pay to keep it, not out of care for the site. Privacy remains: it would move into an encrypted vault only the reader can open, and could be taken elsewhere.

s7.line: Personas are only as good as the articles' graphs
s7.para: With about sixty articles across six topics, the five starting personas each have a real shelf. Richer article graphs make every persona better, so extracting more facts and connections matters. One article, five readers is the first step, sending a librarian, cartographer, historian, explainer and storyteller through each article, with items anchored to sentences.

s8.line: Send your reading and get a designed front page
s8.para: After a few days of normal use, readers can send their reading history: pages, depth, and what they kept, removed or declined. Dinis will reply with a front page designed from it. The page shows everything that would be sent, which can be copied or sent encrypted so only the list agent can read it.

s9.line: Two hypotheses about persona payments, recorded in advance
s9.para: Added to the reading meter's anchors before the first payment, so expectations cannot be rewritten later. H6: when personas follow readers between devices for a price, more readers pay for that than top up for reading alone. H7: readers with more than one persona pay more often than those with one.

s10.line: Try a persona, then see what another device loses
s10.para: Readers can add one of the five personas, keep and remove articles and watch the graph change, then open another device or send their reading. Written on 10 October 2026 from Dinis Cruz's voice note. Figures come from Press Gazette and the Wikimedia Foundation; personas ship in SG Meter v1.1.
